problem: Source "Did I break through one of your rings, that you spread that damned ice on the causeway?" asks whether the ice was her retaliation ("that" = so that / is that why). MODERN "and you spread" turns the causal link into a loose sequence and reads awkwardly.
new_text: "For the men in green—the fairies. It was a perfect moonlit evening for them. Did I break through one of your rings, that you spread that damned ice on the road?"

problem: Source hedge "a little masterful, abrupt, perhaps exacting, sometimes" — the qualifier "sometimes" is dropped.
new_text: "Then, first of all, do you agree that I have some right to be a little commanding, abrupt, perhaps demanding, sometimes, on the grounds I stated—namely, that I am old enough to be your father, and that I have fought through a wide experience with many men of many nations and roamed over half the globe, while you have lived quietly with one group of people in one house?"

problem: Source "a kind of innate sympathy; not the less comforting and encouraging because it is very unobtrusive in its manifestations" = no less comforting for being unobtrusive. MODERN "all the more comforting because it is so quietly given" reverses the logic into a causal intensifier and drops "encouraging".
new_text: "Perfectly clear then—clean and healthy. No flood of foul water had turned it into a poisoned pool. I was your equal at eighteen—quite your equal. Nature meant me to be, on the whole, a good man, Miss Eyre—one of the better kind. And you see I am not. You would say you don't see it; at least I flatter myself I read that much in your eye (beware, by the way, what you express with that eye of yours; I am quick at reading its language). Then take my word for it—I am not a villain. You are not to think that, not to attribute to me any such bad eminence. But, owing I truly believe to circumstances rather than my natural inclination, I am an ordinary, commonplace sinner, worn out by all the petty vices that the rich and worthless use to pass the time. Does it surprise you that I confess this to you? Know that in the course of your future life you will often find yourself elected the involuntary keeper of other people's secrets. They will instinctively discover, as I have done, that it is not your way to talk about yourself, but to listen while others speak of themselves. They will feel, too, that you listen without malicious scorn at their indiscretion, but with a kind of natural sympathy—no less comforting and encouraging for being so quietly given."
